sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Indra** ​(*indra*) — ‌The Storm, ‌the Vajra, ​King of ​the Gods ​· ​the god ​of the ‌atmosphere and ​sky — ​belongs to ‌the Sanskrit ​tradition, ‌where it ​is catalogued ‌under the ​domain "Storms, ​War, Kingship". ​The ​name means ​"the god ‌of the ​atmosphere and ‌sky"[^1].

**Indra** ​is ‌the king ​of the ‌Vedic gods: ​the thunderbolt-bearer ‌who slew ​the ​dragon Vritra ‌and released ‌the rivers, ‌the drinker ​of soma ​who roars ‌into ​battle, the ​thousand-eyed lord ‌of the ​sky. Two ​hundred and ‌fifty ​hymns of ‌the Rigveda ​are addressed ​to him ​— more ​than ‌to any ‌other deity ​— making ‌him the ​best-documented god ​of the ‌ancient ‌world.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌restores the ‌name as ​**Indra** and ‌serves its ​temple ​at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/indra/). The ‌restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form — ​a description ​computed ‌from the ​displayed form ​itself. The ​plain ASCII ‌form *indra* ​survives ‌as a ​modern convenience ‌imposed by ​the early ‌domain-name system; ‌the restoration, ​not ​the fallback, ​is the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The ​name ‌is ‌attested in ​Devanagari ​as ​**इन्द्र**. ​Etymologically ​it ‌means "the ​god ​of ‌the ​atmosphere ‌and ​sky"[^1].

‌The ASCII ​form ​*indra* ​survives ​only ​because ‌the early ​domain-name ‌system ​could ‌not ​carry ‌diacritics; it ​is ‌a ​technological ​compromise, ‌not ‌an ‌ancient spelling. ​The ​Unicode ‌restoration ​**Indra** ​recovers ‌the full ​diacritic ​detail ‌of ​the ‌scholarly ​transliteration directly ​in ​the ​address ‌bar. ‌The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ‌form ​— ​a ‌description ‌computed ‌from ‌the displayed ​form ‌itself.

​The ​letter-by-letter ​transformation ‌runs:

- **i** ​→ ​**I** ​— ‌Same
- ​**n** ​→ **n** ​— ‌Same
- ​**d** ‌→ ​**d** ‌— ​Same
- **r** ‌→ ‌**r** ​— ​Same
- ​**a** ​→ **a** ‌— ‌Short ​/a/

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of the ​name ​is ​**/ˈɪndrə/** ​— ​Sanskrit ‌(IAST: Indra).[^1]

​Phoneme ​by ‌phoneme:

- ​**In-** ‌— ​Short ‌i as ​in ​“bit”, ​followed ​by ​the ‌retroflex dental ​n ‌— ​tongue ‌curled ​back.
- ‌**-dra** — ​The ‌d ​is ​retroflex ‌ḍ ‌in ‌careful speech; ​the ​final ‌a ​is ​a ‌light schwa, ​half-sounded.

​For ‌the ​modern ‌speaker, ​the closest ​approximation ​is: ​“IN-druh” ‌— ‌the ​final vowel ‌breathes ​rather ​than ‌lands

‌Kindred ‌and ‌historical forms ​of ‌the ​name:

- ​**Vedic** ​— ‌Índra
- **Pāli/Prakrit** ​— ​Inda
- ​**Buddhist** ‌— ​Śakra

​One of ​the ‌oldest ​named ‌gods ​in ‌any ​Indo-European language ‌— ‌the ​name ​appears ​already ​in the ‌Rigveda’s ‌first ​hymn.

sections.body:
**Indra** ​is the ‌king of ‌the ​Vedic gods: ​the ​thunderbolt-bearer who ​slew the ​dragon ‌Vritra and ​released the ​rivers, ‌the drinker ​of soma ‌who ​roars into ‌battle, ​the thousand-eyed ​lord of ​the ​sky. Two ​hundred and ‌fifty ​hymns of ‌the Rigveda ​are ‌addressed to ​him ‌— more ​than to ‌any ​other deity ​— making ‌him ‌the best-documented ‌god of ​the ​ancient world.[^1]

### ‌The ​Vajra

The ​thunderbolt forged ‌from ​the bones ​of the ‌sage ​Dadhichi — ‌Indra’s irresistible ​weapon ​against the ​dragon.

### ​Slayer of ‌Vritra

He ‌split ​the dragon ‌that held ​the ​waters captive, ‌and the ‌rivers ‌ran free ‌— ​the founding ‌victory of ​cosmic ​order.

### Lord ​of Soma

‌The ​sacred draught ​that makes ​gods ‌gods: Indra ​drinks ​the soma ​press before ‌every ​battle.

### The ‌Thousand-Eyed

His ​body ‌bears a ​thousand eyes ‌— ‌the marks ​of ​the gods’ ​curse and ​his ‌redemption; the ‌sky’s innumerable ​lights.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated with ‌Indra ​concentrates ​in ​a ​small set ​of ‌recurring ​attributes, ​each ‌a compressed ​statement ‌about ​the ‌name:[^1]

- ​**The Vajra** ​— ​The ​thunderbolt ​forged ‌from the ​bones ‌of ​the ‌sage ​Dadhichi — ‌Indra’s ​irresistible ‌weapon ​against ​the dragon.
- ‌**Slayer ‌of ‌Vritra** ​— ​He split ‌the ​dragon ​that ‌held ​the waters ​captive, ‌and ​the ‌rivers ran ​free ​— ​the ​founding ‌victory of ‌cosmic ​order.
- ‌**Lord ​of ​Soma** — ‌The ‌sacred ‌draught ‌that ​makes gods ‌gods: ​Indra ​drinks ​the ‌soma press ​before ​every ​battle.
- ‌**The ​Thousand-Eyed** — ​His ​body ‌bears ​a ‌thousand eyes ​— ‌the ​marks ‌of ‌the gods’ ​curse ​and ​his ​redemption; ‌the sky’s ‌innumerable ​lights.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The Indra ​of the Rigveda is ‌a storm in divine ‌form: mighty, boisterous, ​sometimes embarrassed, always central. ​His one great ​myth — the combat ​with Vritra — is ​the Vedic creation ‌story: the waters of ​life imprisoned by ​the dragon, the thunderbolt ‌that splits the mountains, ​the rivers released. ‌Everything else in his ​mythology is commentary ‌on that victory.[^1]

### The ​Slaying of Vritra (Rigveda ​1.32)

Vritra, the ​“Enveloper”, coiled about the ​world’s waters and ​held them fast in ‌his mountain caves. Indra, ​armed with the ‌vajra forged by Tvashtri ​from Dadhichi’s bones, ‌struck the dragon on ​its flank; the waters ‌burst free and ​flooded to the sea. ‌‘Like lowing cows ​the waters rushed’ — ​the oldest dragon-slaying in ‌recorded literature, and ‌the template for every ‌one after it.[^2]

### ​The Drink of Soma ​(Rigveda 8)

Before the ‌combat, Indra drinks ​three lakes of soma ​pressed by the ‌priests; filled with the ​draught, his strength is ​irresistible and his ‌belly vast. The hymns ​taunt and flatter ‌him by turns — ​the Vedic poets knew ​their storm-god was ​vain, and loved him ​for it. Soma ‌is both his fuel ‌and his fee.

### The ​Intoxication Hymn (Rigveda ‌10.119)

The most human ​hymn in the ​Rigveda: Indra speaks in ‌the first person, drunk ‌on soma, boasting ‌— ‘I will break ‌the earth’s two ​halves apart, like a ‌gourd I will break ​the two worlds’. ​The gods’ king, for ​one hymn, sounds ‌like a warrior at ​the feast, and the ​poets let him.

### ​From King of Gods ‌to Dethroned Elder ​(Epic & Purāṇic Cycle)

​In the later epics ​the balance shifts: ‌Vishnu’s avatars take the ​great victories, and ‌Indra becomes the anxious ​king who sins — ‌the seducer of ​Ahalyā, the raider of ‌Triparu, the god ‌who must yield his ​throne’s preeminence. The Purāṇas ​preserve a dignity-muted ​Indra, still lord of ​the eastern quarter ‌and of the storm, ‌but no longer the ​cosmos’ protagonist.
